title: Human Electrophysiology in Lab and Operating Room
summary: See how electrical signals are recorded from the human brain, from scalp EEG to electrodes placed during epilepsy surgery and neuromonitoring.

lessons.title: EEG: Cortical Origins, the 10-20 System and Normal Rhythms

levels.kid:
Your brain is full of tiny cells called neurons. They talk to each other with little electrical signals. When lots of them work together, they make a gentle electrical "hum" that we can catch from outside your head!

An **EEG** is a test that listens to that hum. A nurse puts small metal stickers on your scalp. Wires carry the signals to a computer, which draws wiggly lines.

The wiggles change with what you are doing. When you close your eyes and relax, smooth waves called **alpha** waves show up at the back of your head. When you think hard, the waves get small and fast. In deep sleep, they get big and slow, like calm ocean swells.

It doesn't hurt at all. It's like holding a seashell to your ear.
levels.hs:
**Electroencephalography (EEG)** records the brain's electrical activity using electrodes placed on the scalp. Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in 1924 and published it in 1929.

Where does the signal come from? Not mainly from action potentials (the fast spikes neurons fire). It comes from **postsynaptic potentials**: slower voltage changes in the dendrites of **pyramidal neurons** in the cerebral cortex. These neurons are lined up in parallel, like trees in a forest, so when thousands of them are active together, their small currents add up into a signal strong enough to detect through the skull. The scalp signal is tiny, only tens of microvolts (millionths of a volt).

To compare recordings anywhere in the world, electrodes are placed using the **International 10-20 System**. Electrodes sit at 10% or 20% of the distance between skull landmarks: the **nasion** (bridge of the nose), the **inion** (bump at the back of the skull), and the two ears. Letters name the region (F = frontal, C = central, P = parietal, O = occipital, T = temporal). Odd numbers are on the left and even numbers on the right; "z" means midline.

Normal rhythms are grouped by frequency:
- **Delta** (under 4 Hz): deep sleep
- **Theta** (4 to under 8 Hz): drowsiness
- **Alpha** (8 to 13 Hz): relaxed, eyes closed
- **Beta** (over 13 Hz): alert, concentrating

Example: alpha at the back of the head shrinks when you open your eyes. This is called the **Berger effect**.
levels.college:
**Biophysical origin.** Scalp EEG mainly reflects summed **excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials** in cortical **pyramidal cells**. When a synapse on the apical dendrite depolarizes the membrane, current flows into the cell there (a **current sink**) and out elsewhere along the cell (a **source**). This makes an approximate **current dipole**. Pyramidal cells are aligned perpendicular to the cortical surface, so their dipoles add when activity is synchronous. Stellate cells have radially symmetric dendrites and form "closed fields" that cancel. Action potentials contribute little because they are brief (about 1 ms), and nearby spikes rarely overlap in time.

The skull is a poor conductor, so it spatially smears and attenuates the signal. Estimates suggest that around 6 to 10 cm² of synchronously active cortex is needed for a clear scalp spike. Gyral crowns, which lie close to the electrodes, are seen best. Typical amplitudes are about 10 to 100 µV.

**The 10-20 system.** The head is measured from **nasion to inion** and between the **preauricular points**. Electrodes sit at 10% and 20% intervals: Fp1/Fp2, F3/F4, C3/C4, P3/P4, O1/O2, F7/F8, T3/T4 (renamed T7/T8 in the newer 10-10 nomenclature) and T5/T6 (P7/P8), plus Fz, Cz and Pz. Odd numbers are left, even numbers are right.

**Montages.** EEG always measures a voltage *difference*.
- **Bipolar** montages (for example the longitudinal "double banana") chain adjacent electrodes. They localize activity by **phase reversal**.
- **Referential** montages compare each electrode with a common reference (an ear or the average of all electrodes).

**Normal adult rhythms.**
- **Posterior dominant (alpha) rhythm**: 8 to 13 Hz over the occipital region with eyes closed. It is attenuated by eye opening, and it reaches at least 8 Hz by about age 3.
- **Beta**: frontocentral, and increased by benzodiazepines and barbiturates.
- **Mu rhythm**: an arch-shaped 7 to 11 Hz rhythm over C3/C4. It is blocked by movement, or by imagining movement, of the opposite hand.
- **Sleep**: vertex waves and **sleep spindles** (about 11 to 15 Hz) in N2, and high-amplitude delta in N3.
levels.phd:
**Generators and volume conduction.** Under the quasi-static approximation of Maxwell's equations, the scalp potential is a linear superposition of primary currents, shaped by the conductivities of brain, CSF, skull and scalp. The skull has a conductivity roughly 20 to 80 times lower than the brain, and this ratio is still debated. The contribution of a dipole falls off steeply with distance, and its orientation matters: EEG is sensitive to both radial and tangential sources (unlike MEG, which mainly sees tangential ones). Because the transfer is linear, the **inverse problem** (working out the sources from scalp data) has no unique solution. Source models therefore need constraints, such as equivalent current dipoles, minimum-norm estimates or LORETA, together with realistic boundary-element or finite-element head models.

Beyond synaptic currents, other slow membrane events add to the **local field potential** and to EEG: calcium spikes in dendrites, afterhyperpolarizations, and slow glial currents (Buzsáki, Anastassiou and Koch, 2012). Cooper and colleagues' classic simultaneous scalp and cortical recordings (1965) showed how heavily the skull filters high-frequency, spatially focal activity.

**Rhythm generation.**
- **Alpha** depends on thalamocortical loops. Lopes da Silva's studies in dogs implicated thalamic (pulvinar and lateral geniculate) and cortical generators. Hughes and Crunelli described high-threshold bursting thalamocortical cells in the LGN that pace alpha. The modern view treats alpha as active **functional inhibition** (the "gating by inhibition" idea of Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010) rather than simply "idling."
- **Sleep spindles** come from the GABAergic **thalamic reticular nucleus**. They persist in a deafferented reticular nucleus (Steriade). T-type calcium channels allow rebound bursting in thalamocortical cells.
- **Slow oscillations** under 1 Hz in N3 reflect cortical alternation between UP and DOWN states.
- **Gamma** (about 30 to 80 Hz or more) arises from PING/ING interactions between pyramidal cells and parvalbumin-positive basket cells. On scalp EEG it is badly contaminated by muscle activity (Yuval-Greenberg et al., 2008, showed that saccadic spike potentials mimic induced gamma).

**Spectral nuance.** EEG power spectra contain an **aperiodic 1/f component** as well as oscillatory peaks. Methods such as FOOOF/specparam (Donoghue et al., 2020) separate the two. Without this separation, changes in band power can be misread as changes in oscillations.
levels.expert:
**Clinical reading pitfalls.** Many apparent abnormalities on EEG are actually normal variants or artifacts. Readers who over-call them can misdiagnose epilepsy, and the resulting unnecessary antiseizure treatment is a well-documented harm (Benbadis).

Benign variants to recognize include:
- **Wicket spikes** (temporal, arciform, during drowsiness)
- **Small sharp spikes** (benign epileptiform transients of sleep)
- **14 and 6 Hz positive bursts**
- **Rhythmic mid-temporal theta of drowsiness** (formerly "psychomotor variant")
- **Lambda waves** (occipital, when scanning a visual scene)
- **POSTS** (positive occipital sharp transients of sleep)
- **Breach rhythm**

Breach rhythm matters to neurosurgeons. After a craniotomy, the low-resistance skull defect produces higher-amplitude, sharper activity over the defect, which can mimic epileptiform discharges. Artifacts include eye blinks (seen in Fp1/Fp2 because the cornea is positive relative to the retina), glossokinetic artifact, ECG and pulse artifacts, 50/60 Hz mains noise, and electrode "pops."

**Normal findings with clinical weight.**
- A posterior dominant rhythm slower than 8 Hz in an awake adult suggests **encephalopathy**.
- Persistent asymmetry of more than 50% in alpha suggests a structural lesion, which is usually on the lower-amplitude side.
- Excessive diffuse beta should prompt a review of the medication list for drugs that act on GABA-A receptors.
- **Reactivity** (a change in the EEG in response to stimulation) is one of the strongest EEG markers for prognosis after cardiac arrest. Continuous EEG in the ICU uses the American Clinical Neurophysiology Society (ACNS) 2021 terminology (for example GPDs, LPDs and LRDA) to describe patterns on the ictal-interictal continuum.

**Technical standards.** IFCN and ACNS guidelines set expected recording quality, including electrode impedances below about 5 to 10 kΩ, and they promote the denser **10-10** and **10-5** systems for source imaging. High-density EEG (128 to 256 channels) plus individual MRI head models can localize interictal spikes well enough to aid presurgical planning. This works best when it agrees with other evidence such as MRI and seizure semiology.

**Recent advances and open questions.**
- Dry and in-ear electrodes and long-term subscalp EEG devices allow seizure monitoring over months. These recordings have revealed **multidien** (multi-day) seizure cycles that standard short recordings miss.
- Deep-learning classifiers now approach expert-level spike detection, but their performance often drops when moved to new hospitals and recording setups.
- Researchers still debate the biophysical meaning of the aperiodic exponent (it may index the excitation/inhibition balance) and whether gamma activity recorded from the scalp can be trusted.

keyPoints: Scalp EEG mainly reflects synchronized postsynaptic currents in aligned cortical pyramidal cells
Action potentials contribute little because they are brief and rarely overlap in time
The 10-20 system uses nasion, inion and preauricular landmarks; odd numbers are left, even right, z midline
EEG measures voltage differences; bipolar montages localize activity by phase reversal
Normal bands are delta, theta, alpha (8-13 Hz, posterior, blocked by eye opening) and beta
Sleep spindles come from the thalamic reticular nucleus; benign variants and artifacts are often misread

test.q: Which cells generate most of the scalp EEG signal?
test.explain: Pyramidal cells are aligned in parallel, so their dipoles add. Stellate cells form closed fields that cancel out.

test.q: Why do action potentials contribute little to scalp EEG?
choices: They are blocked by cerebrospinal fluid
They occur mainly in white matter tracts
They carry far less charge than ions in glia
They are brief and rarely overlap in time
test.explain: Spikes last about 1 ms, so they seldom summate. The slower postsynaptic potentials do overlap and add up.

test.q: In the 10-20 system, electrode C4 lies over the:
test.explain: C means central and even numbers are on the right. Cz would be the midline position.

test.q: The posterior alpha rhythm is best seen when a person is:
choices: In deep N3 sleep at night
test.explain: Alpha appears over the occipital region in relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed and is blocked by eye opening.

test.q: Which frequency range defines the alpha band?
test.explain: Alpha is 8-13 Hz. Theta is 4 to under 8 Hz, delta is under 4 Hz, and beta is above 13 Hz.

test.q: A bipolar montage localizes a focal discharge by showing:
choices: A flat line at one site
test.explain: In chained bipolar montages, the deflections point toward each other around the electrode nearest the source. This pattern is a phase reversal.

test.q: The mu rhythm over C3 is suppressed by:
test.explain: Mu over the left central region (C3) is blocked by actual or imagined movement of the opposite (right) hand.

test.q: Sleep spindles are generated mainly by the:
test.explain: GABAergic neurons of the thalamic reticular nucleus pace spindles, which can persist even when the nucleus is cut off from its inputs.

test.q: Typical scalp EEG amplitudes are about:
test.explain: Scalp EEG is tiny, tens of microvolts, because the skull attenuates it.

test.q: Which scientist recorded the first human EEG in 1924?
test.explain: Berger also described the alpha rhythm and its blocking when the eyes open.

test.q: In the 10-20 system, the bridge of the nose is the landmark called the ___.
test.explain: Measurements run from the nasion to the inion at the back of the skull.

test.q: Which slow EEG band (under 4 Hz) dominates deep sleep?
test.explain: High-amplitude delta waves characterize N3 sleep.

kidTest.q: What does an EEG listen to?
kidTest.explain: An EEG picks up the brain's tiny electrical hum.

kidTest.q: Where do the EEG stickers go?
kidTest.explain: The electrodes go on your scalp to catch signals from the brain.

kidTest.q: When do alpha waves show up?
choices: When you relax with eyes closed
kidTest.explain: Alpha waves appear when you are relaxed with your eyes closed.

kidTest.q: What do brain waves look like in deep sleep?
kidTest.explain: In deep sleep, the waves are big and slow, like ocean swells.

kidTest.q: Brain cells that send electrical signals are called n _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Neurons talk to each other with tiny electrical signals.

advancedTest.q: Why does a brain region full of stellate cells produce little scalp EEG even when active?
choices: Their action potentials last too long to summate at the scalp
Their radially symmetric dendrites create closed fields that cancel
They release GABA, which carries no transmembrane current
They lie in white matter, beyond the reach of volume conduction
advancedTest.explain: Open-field geometry (aligned pyramidal dendrites) is needed for dipoles to add. Symmetric stellate dendrites produce currents that cancel.

advancedTest.q: After a craniotomy, sharp high-amplitude activity appears over the bone defect. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Mains interference picked up through the surgical scar
An ipsilateral structural lesion lowering alpha
Lambda waves evoked by scanning the room
Breach rhythm from reduced skull attenuation
advancedTest.explain: The skull defect removes a resistive barrier, so activity there looks bigger and sharper. Mistaking it for epileptiform activity is a classic pitfall.

advancedTest.q: A study reports increased beta-band power without modeling the spectrum. What is the main interpretive risk?
choices: Beta increases mostly reflect eye blink artifact at frontal sites
A shift in the aperiodic 1/f slope can mimic an oscillatory change
Beta power rises are usually tied to a matching rise in alpha power
The finding is uninterpretable unless electrode impedance is reported
advancedTest.explain: Band power mixes periodic peaks with the aperiodic component. Methods like specparam separate them.

advancedTest.q: An awake adult has a persistent posterior dominant rhythm slower than 8 Hz. This most suggests:
choices: A normal finding at that age
advancedTest.explain: A posterior rhythm that does not reach 8 Hz in a wakeful adult indicates cerebral dysfunction. Benzodiazepines mainly increase beta.

lessons.title: Evoked Potentials and Event-Related Potentials

levels.kid:
Your brain is always buzzing with tiny electrical signals. It is like a noisy school cafeteria. If you want to hear one quiet friend, that is hard!

Scientists have a trick. They show a flash of light or play a click sound, again and again, hundreds of times. Each time, the brain gives a tiny answer. The answer is the same every time, but the noise is different each time.

When scientists **average** all the answers together, the random noise cancels out. The brain's little answer pops out like a clear wave. This is called an **evoked potential**.

Doctors use it to check if the paths from your eyes, ears and skin to your brain are working, even in babies who cannot talk yet.
levels.hs:
An **evoked potential (EP)** is the brain's electrical response to a specific stimulus, like a flash, a click or a small electric pulse on the wrist. It is recorded with EEG-style electrodes on the scalp.

The problem: these responses are tiny, often just a few microvolts. The ongoing EEG is roughly ten times bigger or more. The solution is **signal averaging**. The stimulus is repeated many times, and the recordings are lined up to the exact moment of each stimulus. The response is **time-locked** (it happens at the same delay every time), while background activity is random. Averaging cancels the random part and keeps the response.

The result is a wave with peaks named by direction and timing. **Latency** is the delay to a peak; **amplitude** is its size. A delayed peak suggests slowed conduction along a nerve pathway.

Three classic clinical EPs:
- **Visual (VEP)**: a checkerboard pattern reverses; a peak near 100 ms (P100) appears over the back of the head.
- **Brainstem auditory (BAEP)**: clicks produce five small waves in the first 10 ms.
- **Somatosensory (SSEP)**: pulses to a nerve at the wrist or ankle.

**Event-related potentials (ERPs)** use the same averaging but study thinking. Example: the **P300**, a positive wave around 300 ms after a rare, surprising target, linked to attention.
levels.college:
Evoked and event-related potentials are stimulus-locked averages of the EEG. Both rely on one assumption: the response is the same on every trial and the background EEG is random noise uncorrelated with the stimulus.

**Why averaging works.** If noise is random, averaging N trials reduces its amplitude by a factor of the square root of N. Averaging 100 trials improves the signal-to-noise ratio about 10-fold; 400 trials, about 20-fold. Small, early brainstem responses need thousands of trials; large cognitive ERPs may need only dozens.

**Naming.** Peaks are labelled by polarity (P or N) and either typical latency in ms (N20, P100, P300) or order (N1, P2). Clinicians mainly measure **latency** and **interpeak intervals**, which are more reliable than amplitude.

**Clinical evoked potentials:**
- **VEP**: pattern-reversal checkerboard; P100 over occipital cortex. A prolonged P100 in one eye is a classic sign of optic neuritis, often seen in multiple sclerosis.
- **BAEP**: waves I-V within about 10 ms. Wave I comes from the distal auditory nerve, wave III roughly from the lower pons (cochlear nucleus/superior olive), wave V roughly from the lateral lemniscus/inferior colliculus. A prolonged I-V interval suggests a brainstem or nerve lesion, such as a vestibular schwannoma. Also used for newborn hearing screening.
- **SSEP**: median nerve stimulation gives a cortical **N20** from primary somatosensory cortex; posterior tibial nerve gives a P37. Pathway: dorsal columns to medial lemniscus to thalamus to cortex.

**Cognitive ERPs:**
- **Mismatch negativity (MMN)**: a deviant sound in a repeated sequence, about 100-250 ms, even without attention.
- **P300 (P3)**: elicited in the **oddball paradigm** by rare targets; amplitude scales with how rare and task-relevant the target is, and latency with how long classification takes.
- **N400**: semantic violations, such as "I take coffee with cream and dog."

EPs test pathway integrity; ERPs probe perception, attention and language with millisecond timing.
levels.phd:
The averaging model treats each trial as signal plus stationary noise. Both assumptions are only approximately true. Latency jitter across trials smears and flattens the average, so an apparent amplitude reduction can reflect variable timing rather than weaker activation. **Woody filtering** and single-trial methods address this. A deeper challenge is the **phase-reset hypothesis** (Makeig and colleagues, 2002): some ERP components may arise partly from stimulus-induced realignment of ongoing oscillations rather than from additive evoked responses. The debate remains unresolved; both mechanisms likely contribute.

**Generators.** Scalp potentials mainly reflect synchronous postsynaptic currents in open-field geometry, chiefly pyramidal cells in cortex. Far-field potentials such as BAEP waves come from volume conduction of synchronous axonal volleys passing through deep structures, and they peak where the current changes direction or crosses a boundary. Assigning a peak to a single nucleus is a simplification; wave V, for example, likely combines several sources.

**Distinguishing evoked from induced activity.** Averaging in the time domain removes activity that is not phase-locked. Time-frequency decomposition of single trials separates **evoked** power (phase-locked) from **induced** power (event-related but not phase-locked), such as gamma or alpha/beta desynchronization. Inter-trial phase coherence quantifies phase locking.

**Classic findings:**
- Sutton, Braren, Zubin and John (1965) discovered the P300 in response to uncertain stimuli.
- Kutas and Hillyard (1980) described the N400 to semantically anomalous words.
- Näätänen and colleagues (1978) characterised MMN, interpreted as a prediction-error signal in predictive-coding frameworks.
- The P300 splits into **P3a** (frontocentral, novelty, orienting) and **P3b** (parietal, target updating). Donchin's context-updating theory links P3b to revising a model of the environment.

**Methodological traps.** Filter settings shift latencies and can create artefactual peaks; strong high-pass filters distort slow waves like the P300 and N400. Reference choice changes topography. Choosing analysis windows after seeing the data inflates false positives, so a priori windows, mass-univariate statistics with cluster correction, and preregistration are now standard practice.
levels.expert:
Clinically, evoked potentials have shrunk as diagnostic tests since MRI arrived, but they remain useful where function rather than structure is the question.

**Diagnostic roles today:**
- VEPs can reveal clinically silent optic nerve involvement, giving evidence of lesions separated in space in suspected demyelinating disease, and they help with unexplained visual loss, including non-organic loss when a normal P100 persists despite claimed blindness.
- BAEPs still serve newborn screening (automated ABR) and estimating hearing thresholds in patients who cannot cooperate, although MRI has replaced them for detecting vestibular schwannoma.
- **Prognosis after cardiac arrest**: bilateral absence of the cortical N20 on median SSEP, with a preserved peripheral (Erb's point) and cervical response, is one of the most specific predictors of poor neurological outcome in comatose survivors. Current guidelines use it within a multimodal approach, combined with imaging, EEG and neuron-specific enolase, never alone. Its sensitivity is limited: a present N20 does not guarantee recovery.

**Pitfalls:**
- Technical failure mimics pathology. Always verify the peripheral and subcortical responses before interpreting a missing cortical wave.
- Hypothermia, temperature and some anesthetic and sedative drugs prolong latencies and reduce cortical amplitudes; muscle artefact can hide an N20, and neuromuscular blockade is sometimes used to reveal it.
- Use lab-specific normative values adjusted for age, height (for lower-limb SSEP) and, for VEPs, check size and luminance.

**Research and translation:**
- ERP-based **brain-computer interfaces**: the P300 speller (Farwell and Donchin, 1988) lets locked-in patients select letters by attending to flashing rows and columns.
- MMN and P300 in disorders of consciousness can reveal covert processing in apparently unresponsive patients, while their absence is uninformative.
- Reduced MMN in schizophrenia is among the most replicated biomarkers and is linked to NMDA receptor function; ketamine reduces MMN in healthy volunteers. It is being studied as a translational marker in drug development.
- Steady-state evoked potentials, such as the 40 Hz auditory response, provide sensitive gamma readouts for testing drugs.

**Open questions:** whether single-trial machine-learning decoding will replace grand averages, and how to standardise ERP pipelines across sites (initiatives such as ERP CORE) to improve reproducibility.

keyPoints: Evoked potentials are tiny brain responses extracted from EEG by stimulus-locked averaging
Averaging N trials reduces random noise by the square root of N
Peaks are named by polarity and latency, e.g. P100, N20, P300
VEP, BAEP and SSEP test the integrity of visual, auditory and somatosensory pathways
ERPs like MMN, P300 and N400 track perception, attention and meaning
Absent bilateral N20 after cardiac arrest predicts poor outcome within multimodal prognosis

test.q: Why are evoked potentials hard to see in a raw EEG trace?
choices: They are much smaller than background activity
They occur at frequencies above human hearing
They appear several minutes after the stimulus
They come from muscles rather than neurons
test.explain: EPs are often a few microvolts, buried in larger ongoing EEG. Averaging is needed to reveal them.

test.q: Averaging 100 trials improves the signal-to-noise ratio by about:
test.explain: Random noise falls by the square root of N, and the square root of 100 is 10.

test.q: A prolonged P100 in one eye on visual evoked potential testing suggests:
choices: Slowed conduction in that optic nerve
Hearing loss in the opposite ear
test.explain: A delayed P100 indicates slowed optic nerve conduction, as in optic neuritis.

test.q: Brainstem auditory evoked potential waves I-V occur within roughly:
test.explain: BAEP waves are very early, within about 10 ms of the click.

test.q: The N20 after median nerve stimulation comes mainly from:
choices: Primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe
Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellar cortex
Cochlear division of the vestibulocochlear nerve
test.explain: The N20 is the cortical somatosensory response from the primary somatosensory cortex contralateral to the stimulated median nerve.

test.q: In the oddball paradigm, a rare target stimulus typically produces a:
test.explain: The P300 appears around 300 ms after rare, task-relevant targets.

test.q: The sentence "I take coffee with cream and dog" is designed to elicit the:
test.explain: The N400 tracks semantic violations, such as a word that does not fit its context.

test.q: Which response can be elicited by a deviant sound even without attention?
test.explain: MMN arises automatically to deviant sounds in a repeating sequence, even when attention is directed elsewhere.

test.q: Clinicians rely most on which evoked potential measures?
test.explain: Latency and interpeak intervals are more reliable than amplitude.

test.q: Evoked responses are ___-locked: they occur at the same delay after every stimulus.
test.explain: Time locking lets averaging keep the response while cancelling random noise.

test.q: What is the term for the delay from the stimulus to a peak?
test.explain: Latency reflects conduction time along the pathway.

test.q: What abbreviation names the evoked potential produced by stimulating a nerve at the wrist?
test.explain: Somatosensory evoked potentials test the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.

kidTest.q: Why do scientists repeat the flash or click many times?
choices: So the person gets very sleepy
So the brain answers can be averaged
So the machine can warm up
kidTest.explain: Averaging many answers makes the noise cancel out.

kidTest.q: What happens to the random noise when answers are averaged?
kidTest.explain: Random noise is different each time, so it cancels.

kidTest.q: What does an evoked potential help doctors check?
choices: How tall a child will grow
Whether paths to the brain work
kidTest.explain: It checks paths from eyes, ears and skin to the brain.

kidTest.q: Who can be tested even if they cannot talk yet?
kidTest.explain: The test does not need the person to answer out loud.

kidTest.q: Scientists add the answers together and find the a _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Averaging makes the brain's small answer pop out.

advancedTest.q: An ERP component is smaller in patients than in controls. Which alternative explanation is most important to rule out?
choices: Higher skull conductivity in patients boosting far-field waves
Patients producing more phase-locked gamma than controls
Controls having slower conduction in the auditory nerve
Greater trial-to-trial latency jitter in patients smearing the average
advancedTest.explain: Latency jitter flattens averaged peaks, mimicking weaker activation. Single-trial methods or Woody filtering can test this.

advancedTest.q: A comatose post-arrest patient lacks cortical N20s, but Erb's point and cervical responses are also absent. The best interpretation is:
choices: Evidence of a selective brainstem lesion that spares the cortex
A technical or peripheral failure, leaving it uninterpretable
Strong evidence of a poor neurological outcome after the arrest
Proof of covert awareness persisting in the unresponsive patient
advancedTest.explain: Absent peripheral responses mean the volley never reached the cortex, so a missing N20 cannot be interpreted as cortical failure.

advancedTest.q: Gamma activity increases after a stimulus, but the averaged ERP shows nothing. This pattern best indicates:
choices: An artefact created by reference choice
Mismatch negativity overlapping with the P3a
Evoked activity that is strongly phase-locked
Induced activity that is not phase-locked
advancedTest.explain: Time-domain averaging cancels non-phase-locked activity. Induced power is revealed by single-trial time-frequency analysis.

advancedTest.q: Why is mismatch negativity attractive as a translational marker in schizophrenia drug development?
choices: It is produced mainly by the brainstem cochlear nucleus
It requires active attention and verbal reports
It increases in size during ketamine administration
It is reliably reduced and sensitive to NMDA receptor manipulation
advancedTest.explain: MMN is a replicated reduction in schizophrenia and is decreased by ketamine, linking it to NMDA function measurable across species and in trials.

lessons.title: Magnetoencephalography (MEG): Recording the Brain's Magnetic Fields

levels.kid:
When electricity flows through a wire, it makes a tiny magnetic field around it. Your brain cells send electricity too, so your brain makes magnetic fields!

These fields are super, super weak. The Earth's magnetism is about a billion times stronger. So scientists built a special machine called **MEG**. It looks like a giant hair dryer helmet. Inside are sensors so sensitive they must be kept colder than outer space.

The room around it is a special shielded box that keeps out outside magnetic "noise" from cars and elevators.

MEG doesn't hurt at all. It just listens. It can tell doctors when, and where, parts of your brain are working, almost as fast as you think.
levels.hs:
**Magnetoencephalography (MEG)** measures the tiny magnetic fields produced by electrical currents in the brain. Whenever current flows, a magnetic field forms around it. That is the same physics as an electromagnet.

The main source is not single spikes but **synchronized currents** in thousands of **pyramidal neurons** in the cortex, flowing inside their long dendrites. Roughly tens of thousands of neurons must be active together to produce a measurable signal.

These fields are tiny: about 10 to 1,000 **femtotesla** (fT). Earth's magnetic field is about 50 microtesla, roughly a billion times bigger. MEG therefore needs two things:
- Extremely sensitive sensors called **SQUIDs** (superconducting quantum interference devices), cooled in liquid helium to about 4 kelvin (-269 °C).
- A **magnetically shielded room** with walls of special metal alloys to block outside fields.

MEG has **millisecond timing**, like EEG. Magnetic fields are barely distorted by the skull and scalp, so MEG can locate sources more precisely than EEG.

A real example: before epilepsy surgery, MEG can find where abnormal spikes start. It can also map areas for movement, touch and language so surgeons can avoid them. The test is silent and painless, with no radiation or injections.
levels.college:
MEG records magnetic fields produced by **primary (intracellular) currents** in neurons, chiefly the dendrites of cortical pyramidal cells. These cells are aligned in parallel, so their synchronized **postsynaptic currents** sum into a measurable **current dipole**. A detectable source is estimated at roughly 10 nA·m, which corresponds to about 50,000 or more coactive neurons. Action potentials contribute less. Their brief, opposing currents form quadrupoles that cancel over distance.

**MEG vs EEG**
- EEG mainly reflects **volume currents** in tissue, which are smeared by the low-conductivity skull. MEG fields pass through skull and scalp almost undistorted, which simplifies modeling.
- MEG mostly sees **tangential** sources, such as dipoles in the walls of sulci. A perfectly radial dipole in a spherical head makes no external field, so crown-of-gyrus sources are weak in MEG but visible in EEG. The two methods are complementary and are often recorded together.
- MEG falls off steeply with depth, so deep structures are hard to detect.

**Hardware**
- Whole-head systems hold about 300 SQUID sensors in a liquid-helium **dewar**.
- **Magnetometers** measure the field directly. **Gradiometers** measure spatial differences, which rejects distant noise.
- A **magnetically shielded room** uses mu-metal layers and aluminum.

**Source localization** is an **inverse problem**. Many current patterns can produce the same external field, so it has no unique solution. Analysts add constraints in two main ways:
- **Equivalent current dipole (ECD)** fitting models the activity as one or a few point sources.
- **Distributed methods** such as minimum-norm estimates (MNE, dSPM, sLORETA) and **beamformers** estimate activity across the whole cortex.

Results are coregistered onto the patient's MRI to produce **magnetic source imaging (MSI)**.

**Clinical uses** include localizing interictal epileptiform spikes and presurgical functional mapping of somatosensory, motor, auditory, visual and language cortex.
levels.phd:
MEG physics rests on the **quasi-static approximation** of Maxwell's equations. At neural frequencies (below about 1 kHz), capacitive and inductive effects are negligible. The measured field B arises from the primary current J_p plus volume currents shaped by conductivity, as described by the Biot–Savart law.

Two results from the **Sarvas (1987)** spherical-model solution are central:
- Radial dipoles produce no external field.
- In a spherically symmetric conductor, conductivity does not affect the external radial field at all.

Together these explain why MEG forward models are simpler than EEG models, often a single-shell or boundary-element model of the inner skull. The forward lead field scales roughly with 1/r², so sensitivity drops sharply with source depth.

The field began with **David Cohen** (1968), who used an induction coil to record alpha rhythm. In 1972 he used Zimmerman's **SQUID** in MIT's shielded room. A DC SQUID is a superconducting loop with two **Josephson junctions**. It converts flux into voltage with a periodicity of one flux quantum (Φ0 = h/2e ≈ 2.07 × 10⁻¹⁵ Wb). It is run in a flux-locked loop and coupled to pickup coils. Typical white noise is about 3–5 fT/√Hz.

**Inverse solutions**
- The neuroelectromagnetic inverse problem is ill-posed, as Helmholtz showed in 1853.
- ECD fitting minimizes residual variance, judged by goodness-of-fit.
- **Minimum-norm** estimation (Hämäläinen & Ilmoniemi) is regularized least squares and biases solutions toward superficial sources. Depth-weighting and noise-normalization (dSPM, sLORETA) partly correct this.
- **LCMV beamformers** (Van Veen 1997) spatially filter each location. They fail for highly correlated sources, such as bilateral auditory responses.

**Noise handling** includes **signal-space separation** and its temporal extension tSSS (Taulu). These use spherical-harmonic expansions to split internal from external field components. ICA removes cardiac and ocular artifacts.

On the controversy over deep sources, simulations and recordings suggest hippocampal and amygdalar activity can sometimes be detected. This is still debated because leakage from overlying cortex can mimic it.

Canonical findings include the **M100/N100m** auditory response with tonotopy, somatosensory **M20**, and beta **event-related desynchronization** with post-movement rebound in sensorimotor cortex.
levels.expert:
Clinically, MEG/MSI is most established in **presurgical epilepsy evaluation**. The American Clinical MEG Society (ACMEGS) clinical practice guidelines cover recording and interpretation of interictal spikes and mapping of eloquent cortex. Spike dipole **clusters** carry more weight than scattered dipoles. In outcome studies, resecting a tight cluster correlates with seizure freedom. MEG is especially valuable in two situations:
- **MRI-negative** focal epilepsy, where it can redirect review of MRI and help find subtle focal cortical dysplasia.
- Planning where to place **stereo-EEG** electrodes. MEG generates hypotheses for implantation rather than replacing invasive recording.

Practical pitfalls:
- Ictal capture is rare, because the patient must stay still in the helmet for limited sessions. Interpretation therefore relies on interictal spikes, which are irritative-zone, not seizure-onset, markers.
- Radial or crown-of-gyrus and mesial temporal generators can be missed. Simultaneous EEG helps.
- Magnetic artifacts come from dental work, vagus nerve stimulators, shunt valves and implanted hardware. tSSS mitigates but does not eliminate these.
- Head movement degrades localization. Continuous head-position indicator coils allow correction.
- Dipoles that fit with poor goodness-of-fit, or that are forced onto propagated activity, mislead.

For **eloquent mapping**, MEG measures language **lateralization** using receptive-language paradigms with late-window source counts. It can partly substitute for the invasive intracarotid amobarbital (Wada) test and agrees with it in most series. Discordance warrants Wada or fMRI. MEG maps of the central sulcus from somatosensory evoked fields help surgeons plan around tumors where anatomy is distorted. This is valuable because MEG reflects neural current directly. fMRI relies on a hemodynamic signal, which can be unreliable near tumors.

A major recent advance is **optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs)**. These alkali-vapor sensors work in spin-exchange-relaxation-free mode near room temperature, so they need no helium. They mount on the scalp, closer to the brain, which boosts signal. Wearable OPM-MEG (Boto et al., Nature 2018) lets subjects move and suits children. It requires active field nulling coils, and sensor counts and bandwidth are still maturing. Helium scarcity has also driven helium-recycling systems.

Open questions include reliable deep-source and high-frequency oscillation detection, validated connectivity metrics that are robust to source leakage, and broader billing and outcome evidence outside epilepsy, for example in TBI and psychiatric biomarkers.

keyPoints: MEG measures magnetic fields from synchronized dendritic currents in cortical pyramidal neurons
Brain fields are femtotesla-scale, about a billion times weaker than Earth's field
SQUIDs in liquid helium plus a magnetically shielded room make detection possible
MEG sees tangential (sulcal) sources best; radial and deep sources are weak
Source localization is an ill-posed inverse problem solved with dipoles, minimum-norm or beamformers
Clinical use: localizing epileptic spikes and mapping eloquent cortex; OPMs enable wearable MEG

test.q: What is the main source of the MEG signal?
choices: Ion pump currents in surrounding glial cells
Blood flow changes in active cortical areas
Brief action potentials traveling along axons
test.explain: Summed postsynaptic currents in aligned pyramidal dendrites form a measurable dipole. Spike fields largely cancel over distance.

test.q: Roughly how strong are brain magnetic fields measured by MEG?
test.explain: MEG signals are about 10 to 1,000 fT. Microtesla is the scale of Earth's field.

test.q: Why are MEG sensors bathed in liquid helium?
choices: To magnetize the patient's head tissue
To slow down the neurons for imaging
To keep the scalp from overheating
test.explain: SQUIDs only work when superconducting, which requires temperatures near 4 kelvin.

test.q: Which source orientation is hardest for MEG to detect?
test.explain: A radial dipole in a spherical head produces little or no external magnetic field, so EEG sees it better.

test.q: Why does MEG localize cortical sources more easily than EEG?
choices: Its sensors sit inside the skull itself
It detects deep brain activity especially well
Magnetic fields pass the skull nearly undistorted
It samples far faster than any EEG system
test.explain: The low-conductivity skull smears EEG volume currents, but barely affects magnetic fields. Deep sources are actually weak in MEG.

test.q: What is the purpose of the magnetically shielded room?
choices: To cool the sensors to low temperature
To keep the patient's head still
test.explain: Environmental fields from Earth, traffic and elevators dwarf brain signals, so mu-metal shielding blocks them.

test.q: Why is MEG source localization called an ill-posed inverse problem?
choices: The MRI scan is usually taken on a later day
Magnetic fields reverse direction in the skull
Many current patterns can fit the same field
The sensors record too slowly to resolve it
test.explain: There is no unique solution, so constraints like dipole models or minimum-norm assumptions are needed.

test.q: Which is a major clinical use of MEG?
choices: Estimating cerebral blood volume in stroke
test.explain: MEG helps find where interictal spikes arise and maps eloquent cortex before epilepsy surgery.

test.q: What does a gradiometer measure?
choices: The voltage between two scalp sites
The field's spatial difference across coils
The oxygen level in local blood
test.explain: Gradiometers measure field differences, which reject distant noise sources whose fields are nearly uniform.

test.q: What is the acronym for the superconducting sensors used in traditional MEG?
test.explain: SQUID stands for superconducting quantum interference device.

test.q: MEG results coregistered onto a patient's MRI are called magnetic source ___.
test.explain: This is magnetic source imaging, or MSI.

test.q: Like EEG, MEG has excellent temporal resolution, on the order of a ___.
test.explain: MEG tracks neural activity at millisecond timescales.

kidTest.q: What does MEG measure?
choices: Heat given off by the skin of the head
The total weight of the brain tissue
Magnetic fields made by the brain
kidTest.explain: Brain electricity makes tiny magnetic fields, and MEG senses them.

kidTest.q: How strong are the brain's magnetic fields?
kidTest.explain: They are about a billion times weaker than Earth's magnetism.

kidTest.q: Why is the MEG room a special shielded box?
choices: To make the machine feel warm
To keep out outside magnetic noise
To keep the room very bright
kidTest.explain: The box blocks magnetic noise from things like cars and elevators.

kidTest.q: How does an MEG test feel?
kidTest.explain: MEG just listens, so it is painless.

kidTest.q: MEG sensors must be kept very c _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The sensors are kept colder than outer space.

advancedTest.q: A patient's spikes arise from a gyral crown and are seen clearly on EEG but not on MEG. The best explanation is:
choices: The skull blocks magnetic fields more strongly than electric potentials
A radial dipole produces almost no external field in a near-spherical head
MEG lacks the temporal resolution to capture brief interictal spikes
SQUIDs saturate when sources sit close to the cortical surface
advancedTest.explain: Radial sources are nearly magnetically silent (Sarvas). The skull actually distorts EEG, not MEG.

advancedTest.q: An LCMV beamformer shows weak, mislocalized auditory responses to binaural tones. The most likely cause is:
choices: Helium boil-off raising the sensor noise floor
Strongly correlated bilateral sources canceling in the spatial filter
Excess depth-weighting pushing activity toward the brainstem
Radial orientation of sources in Heschl's gyrus
advancedTest.explain: Beamformers assume uncorrelated sources. Synchronous bilateral auditory cortices partially cancel each other.

advancedTest.q: Why do unweighted minimum-norm estimates tend to misplace deep activity superficially?
choices: Deep sources produce radial fields that the model ignores
The skull conductivity is set too high in such models
Lead fields fall with depth, so superficial currents fit with less power
Volume currents dominate deep sources in the forward model
advancedTest.explain: Minimizing current norm favors superficial sources, which explain the data with less current. dSPM and sLORETA normalize for this.

advancedTest.q: Why do on-scalp OPM sensors boost signal relative to SQUID helmets?
choices: They suppress volume currents that cancel the primary currents
They detect electric potentials in addition to magnetic fields
They sit closer to the cortex, and the field falls steeply with distance
They operate at higher frequencies where neural power is greater
advancedTest.explain: SQUIDs sit behind a cryogenic gap. OPMs on the scalp reduce source-sensor distance, and field strength rises sharply as that distance shrinks.

lessons.title: ECoG and Stereo-EEG for Epilepsy Surgery

levels.kid:
Some kids and grown-ups have **seizures**. A seizure is like an electrical storm in the brain. Medicines stop the storms for most people, but not for everyone.

If medicine doesn't work, doctors may try surgery. First they must find exactly where the storm starts. It's like finding which smoke alarm in a big house goes off first.

So doctors put tiny listening wires right on or inside the brain. Some are flat sheets laid on top, like stickers. Others are thin threads that go deep inside, like pins in a pincushion.

The person stays in the hospital for days while the wires listen. When a seizure happens, doctors see where it began. Then they can plan how to stop it.
levels.hs:
**Epilepsy** means repeated seizures caused by bursts of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. About one in three people with epilepsy keep having seizures even after trying two suitable medicines. This is called **drug-resistant epilepsy**. For some of these patients, surgery to remove or disconnect the place where seizures start can stop them.

That place is called the **seizure onset zone**. Scalp EEG and MRI often can't locate it precisely, because the skull blurs electrical signals and some areas lie deep inside the brain. So surgeons record from inside the head, which is called **intracranial EEG**. There are two main methods:
- **ECoG (electrocorticography)**: flat grids and strips of disc electrodes placed on the brain's surface. This requires a large opening in the skull called a **craniotomy**.
- **Stereo-EEG (SEEG)**: thin depth electrodes, each with many contacts along it, put in through tiny drill holes. They reach deep structures in three dimensions.

Patients are then monitored with video for days to weeks, often while their medicines are lowered so seizures happen. Example: a teenager with seizures that start with a strange rising feeling in the stomach might get SEEG electrodes in both hippocampi. If every seizure starts in the left hippocampus, removing that area can make the person seizure-free.
levels.college:
Intracranial EEG (iEEG) is used in **phase II** of a presurgical evaluation. Phase I is noninvasive: video-EEG, MRI, neuropsychology, and often PET, SPECT or MEG. When these disagree or point to a region that needs closer mapping, iEEG tests a specific hypothesis about where seizures begin.

**Why record inside the skull?** Scalp EEG needs roughly 6-10 cm² of synchronously active cortex to show a clear spike, and it is weighted toward the convexity. Intracranial contacts sit millimeters from the generators, giving microvolt-to-millivolt signals with far better spatial resolution and access to high frequencies.

**Subdural grids and strips (ECoG):**
- Platinum or stainless steel discs, usually about 2-4 mm across, spaced about 1 cm apart in silicone sheets.
- Dense 2D coverage of the cortical surface, which is ideal for mapping eloquent cortex next to a lesion.
- Weaknesses: requires a craniotomy, samples sulcal depths and deep structures poorly, and is hard to place on both sides of the brain.

**Stereo-EEG:**
- Pioneered by Talairach and Bancaud in Paris in the 1950s-60s.
- Each depth electrode is about 0.8 mm wide with 5-18 contacts. Typically 8-20 electrodes are placed through twist-drill holes using a frame or robot.
- Samples deep structures (hippocampus, insula, cingulate) and sulcal depths across both hemispheres.
- Coverage is sparse, so a well-reasoned implantation hypothesis is essential.

**What clinicians look for:**
- The **ictal onset pattern**, such as low-voltage fast activity or preictal spiking.
- Which contacts are involved first, and how activity spreads.
- **Interictal** spikes and **high-frequency oscillations** (HFOs).

The results guide resection, laser ablation, or neuromodulation. SEEG has become the dominant method in North America over the last 15 years, largely because it has fewer complications than grids.
levels.phd:
The iEEG signal is the local field potential: summed synaptic and dendritic currents. Bipolar montages between neighboring contacts sample only a few millimeters of tissue, while referential recordings pick up activity from farther away through volume conduction. This matters in SEEG, where a contact in white matter can still record cortical activity. Co-registering CT and MRI to localize each contact is therefore essential.

**Conceptual zones** (Rosenow and Lüders, 2001): the epileptogenic zone is the theoretical minimum tissue whose removal produces seizure freedom. It cannot be measured directly and is estimated from the seizure onset zone, the irritative zone (where interictal spikes occur), lesions, and symptoms. The Paris school instead framed seizures as an **epileptogenic network** organized in space and time, which shapes SEEG implantation strategy.

**Ictal onset patterns:** low-voltage fast activity (gamma, above about 30 Hz) is linked to focal onset and better outcomes after resection. Low-frequency rhythmic spiking is typical of mesial temporal sclerosis. Bartolomei's **Epileptogenicity Index** quantifies how strongly and how early fast activity appears on each channel.

**HFOs:** ripples (80-250 Hz) and fast ripples (250-500 Hz) were first described in human hippocampus by Bragin and Engel in 1999. Fast ripples are thought to reflect out-of-phase firing of pathologically interconnected neurons. Retrospective studies suggested that removing HFO-generating tissue predicts good outcomes. However, the randomized HFO trial (Zijlmans group, 2022) failed to show that HFO-guided ECoG was non-inferior to spike-guided surgery. Physiological ripples, especially in hippocampus and occipital cortex, also confound interpretation.

**Comparative safety:** meta-analyses estimate SEEG hemorrhage at about 1% and infection below 1%, lower than for subdural grids, which also carry risks of edema and raised pressure. In Europe, SEEG combined with radiofrequency thermocoagulation through the implanted contacts can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Outcomes depend on the substrate. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy carries roughly a 60-70% chance of seizure freedom (Wiebe 2001 RCT). MRI-negative neocortical epilepsy has lower rates.
levels.expert:
**Implantation planning.** A strong SEEG plan tests competing hypotheses, not just the leading one. For an MRI-negative case with possible insular or opercular onset, each trajectory should sample the presumed onset, early spread sites, and the alternative, such as orbitofrontal or temporal pole. Robotic systems (ROSA, Neuromate) achieve entry and target errors of about 1-2 mm. Avascular trajectory planning on contrast MRI or CTA is the main defense against hemorrhage.

**Pitfalls in interpretation:**
- Recording from spread rather than onset. If the first change is rhythmic activity rather than fast activity, or if symptoms appear before any electrographic change, suspect the true onset lies outside the sampled area.
- Lowering medicines can bring out atypical, secondarily generalized seizures. Habitual seizures are what matter.
- Bilateral independent hippocampal onsets argue for responsive neurostimulation rather than resection.

**Intraoperative ECoG** is a separate use: brief recordings at surgery to tailor resections, for example around focal cortical dysplasia or in tumor-related epilepsy. Residual spiking after resection gives limited and debated prognostic information.

**Beyond resection.** iEEG findings increasingly guide minimally invasive or nondestructive options. These include MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy and hypothalamic hamartoma, and responsive neurostimulation (RNS, NeuroPace), which itself records long-term ambulatory ECoG. RNS data revealed multidien (multiday) seizure cycles (Baud et al., 2018), which changed ideas about seizure forecasting. Thalamic SEEG sampling, mainly of the anterior and centromedian nuclei, is spreading to guide deep brain stimulation and RNS targeting.

**Research windfall.** Epilepsy monitoring units provide rare human single-neuron and LFP data. Microwire Behnke-Fried electrodes yielded concept cells (Quiroga 2005), and high-gamma ECoG underpins speech BCIs.

**Open questions:**
- Can network models, such as virtual epileptic patient simulations (EPINOV trial), outperform expert visual reading?
- How should HFOs be validated prospectively?
- How much spatial undersampling is acceptable?
- How should invasive monitoring be weighed against high-resolution MEG and 7T MRI in children?

Many specialists consider epilepsy surgery underused, with referral delays of about 20 years.

keyPoints: Intracranial EEG localizes the seizure onset zone in drug-resistant epilepsy
ECoG uses subdural grids and strips on the cortical surface via craniotomy
Stereo-EEG uses depth electrodes through small drill holes for 3D, deep, bilateral sampling
Low-voltage fast activity at onset suggests a focal, resectable onset
HFOs are promising biomarkers but were not validated in a randomized trial
Results guide resection, laser ablation, or responsive neurostimulation

test.q: Why is intracranial EEG needed in some epilepsy surgery candidates?
choices: Intracranial recording replaces the need for MRI
The skull and depth limit localization by scalp EEG
Seizure medications block scalp EEG signals
Scalp EEG fails to record seizure activity of any kind
test.explain: The skull blurs signals and deep regions are poorly seen, so recording closer to the brain improves localization.

test.q: Which describes stereo-EEG?
choices: Silicone grids laid over the cortical convexity
Scalp electrodes arranged in a dense high-density cap
Magnetic sensors placed around the outside of the head
Depth electrodes inserted through small drill holes
test.explain: SEEG uses thin multicontact depth electrodes placed through twist-drill holes.

test.q: A key advantage of subdural grids over SEEG is:
choices: No need to open the skull
test.explain: Grids give continuous surface coverage, which helps with mapping, but they need a craniotomy and sample deep areas poorly.

test.q: Drug-resistant epilepsy is usually defined as failure of:
choices: Three surgical procedures in a row
One medication taken for a single month
test.explain: Failure of two appropriate, tolerated medication trials defines drug resistance.

test.q: Which deep structure is a common SEEG target in temporal lobe epilepsy?
test.explain: Mesial temporal epilepsy often arises from the hippocampus, which SEEG can sample directly.

test.q: Which ictal onset pattern is linked to focal onset and good surgical outcome?
test.explain: Low-voltage fast (gamma) activity at onset is associated with focal onset and better outcomes.

test.q: Why are medications often reduced during intracranial monitoring?
choices: To lower the risk of electrode infection
To make recording seizures more likely
To improve how well electrodes conduct signals
To shorten the time needed for implantation
test.explain: Fewer medicines make seizures more likely during the limited monitoring window.

test.q: Ripples and fast ripples are types of:
test.explain: Ripples (80-250 Hz) and fast ripples (250-500 Hz) are high-frequency oscillations.

test.q: Compared with subdural grids, SEEG is generally associated with:
test.explain: Meta-analyses show lower complication rates for SEEG than for grids.

test.q: The region where seizures begin is called the seizure onset ___.
test.explain: The seizure onset zone is the main target identified by intracranial EEG.

test.q: What large skull opening is needed to place subdural grids?
test.explain: Grids need a craniotomy, while SEEG uses small drill holes.

test.q: Which French researcher pioneered SEEG together with Bancaud?
test.explain: Talairach and Bancaud developed SEEG in Paris in the 1950s-60s.

kidTest.q: What is a seizure like?
choices: A cold that makes you sneeze
A broken bone in the arm
An electrical storm in the brain
kidTest.explain: A seizure is a burst of unusual electrical activity in the brain.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors put listening wires on the brain?
choices: To help the person sleep better
To give the brain more energy
kidTest.explain: The wires show the exact spot where the storm begins.

kidTest.q: Which wires go deep inside the brain?
kidTest.explain: Thin depth threads reach deep places.

kidTest.q: When do doctors usually try this surgery?
choices: When someone has a sore throat
kidTest.explain: Surgery is for people whose seizures keep happening despite medicine.

kidTest.q: The wires listen for a s _ _ _ _ _ _ to see where it begins.
kidTest.explain: Doctors wait for a seizure to see where it starts.

advancedTest.q: On SEEG, the first change is slow rhythmic activity, and symptoms began before any electrographic change. The best inference is:
choices: The electrodes need replacing for poor impedance
The true onset may lie outside the sampled region
The onset contact should be resected right away
The patient most likely has generalized epilepsy
advancedTest.explain: Symptoms before any EEG change, with slow rather than fast activity first, suggest the electrodes recorded spread, not the onset.

advancedTest.q: Why is bipolar referencing especially important for interpreting SEEG?
choices: It confines the signal to tissue near adjacent contacts
It removes the need to co-register CT with MRI
It allows electrodes to be placed in larger numbers
It boosts volume-conducted signals from distant cortex
advancedTest.explain: Bipolar derivations cancel shared distant activity, which reduces the confusion caused by volume conduction.

advancedTest.q: SEEG shows independent seizure onsets in both hippocampi. Which option is most appropriate?
choices: Resecting whichever side has more spikes
Removal of both temporal lobes at once
Repeating SEEG with grid electrodes instead
advancedTest.explain: Removing both hippocampi risks severe memory loss, so responsive neurostimulation is preferred for bilateral independent onsets.

advancedTest.q: What did the randomized HFO trial imply about HFO-guided surgery?
choices: HFO guidance was not shown non-inferior to spike guidance
HFOs proved useless and unrelated to epileptic tissue
HFOs showed superiority and became the standard of care
HFOs were shown to be identical to physiological ripples
advancedTest.explain: The trial failed to show non-inferiority, so HFOs remain promising but not validated. Retrospective data still link them to epileptic tissue.

lessons.title: Intraoperative Neuromonitoring and Cortical Stimulation Mapping

levels.kid:
Imagine fixing a toy that is full of tiny wires. You would want to know which wires make the lights work, so you don't cut them by mistake.

Brain surgeons have the same problem. Some parts of the brain move your hand. Some parts help you talk. During surgery, doctors use special tools to listen to the brain and the nerves. If a signal starts to fade, an alarm tells the surgeon to stop and check.

Sometimes the patient is even awake! The doctor gives a tiny, safe buzz to one spot of the brain. If the patient suddenly can't name a picture, that spot is important for talking. The surgeon leaves it alone.

This way, doctors can take out the bad part and keep the good parts safe.
levels.hs:
**Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM)** means recording nervous system signals during surgery to catch injury early, while it can still be reversed. A team of neurophysiologists watches the signals while the surgeon works.

Main tools:
- **Motor evoked potentials (MEPs)**: the motor cortex is stimulated through electrodes on the scalp or brain surface, and muscle responses are recorded. A big drop suggests the motor pathway is in danger.
- **Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs)**: a nerve in the wrist or ankle is stimulated, and the signal is recorded as it reaches the brain.
- **Electromyography (EMG)**: records muscle activity to warn when a nerve is being stretched or irritated.

**Cortical stimulation mapping** finds the brain areas that must be kept. The surgeon touches the cortex with a probe that delivers a small electrical current. Over the motor cortex this causes a twitch. Over language areas, the patient is kept **awake** and asked to name pictures or count. If stimulating a spot briefly stops their speech, that spot is labeled essential.

Example: a patient has a tumor called a glioma near **Broca's area**, a region for producing speech. In an **awake craniotomy**, mapping lets the surgeon remove as much tumor as possible while sparing the spots that stop speech. That gives the patient a longer life without losing language.
levels.college:
IONM and stimulation mapping turn the electrophysiology of evoked potentials into real-time safety tools. They serve two jobs. **Monitoring** checks that a pathway still works. **Mapping** locates a structure so it can be avoided.

**Monitoring modalities**
- **Transcranial MEPs**: brief high-voltage pulse trains are delivered through corkscrew scalp electrodes over the motor cortex, and compound muscle action potentials are recorded from limb muscles. MEPs test the corticospinal tract and are key in spinal cord and brainstem surgery.
- **SSEPs**: median or posterior tibial nerve stimulation, recorded over the cortex. Warning criteria are usually about a 50% amplitude drop or a 10% latency increase. SSEPs test the dorsal columns, not motor pathways, so a motor injury can be missed.
- **Free-run and triggered EMG**: detect nerve irritation and help confirm pedicle screw position. In skull base surgery they protect cranial nerves such as the facial nerve.
- **Brainstem auditory evoked potentials** protect the hearing pathway, for example during acoustic neuroma resection.

**Anesthesia matters.** Volatile anesthetics depress cortical SSEPs and MEPs. Neuromuscular blockers abolish MEPs and EMG. Total intravenous anesthesia, for example with propofol and remifentanil, is preferred.

**Direct cortical stimulation**
- **Penfield technique**: 50-60 Hz biphasic pulses delivered through a bipolar probe with tips about 5 mm apart, for a few seconds per site.
- **Train-of-five technique**: high-frequency short trains given through a monopolar probe, recording MEPs. It works under general anesthesia and causes fewer seizures.
- **Language mapping** in awake patients uses picture naming, counting and reading. A site is called positive if stimulating it disrupts the task reproducibly.
- **Afterdischarges** on electrocorticography warn of an impending seizure. Cold irrigation on the cortex stops stimulation-induced seizures.
levels.phd:
Cortical stimulation mapping descends from Wilder Penfield and colleagues at the Montreal Neurological Institute in the 1930s-50s. Their stimulation of awake epilepsy patients produced the motor and sensory homunculi and the first systematic maps of speech arrest. Ojemann's 1989 study of 117 patients overturned the textbook picture of one fixed Broca's and Wernicke's area. Essential language sites were small, often 1-2 cm², and highly variable between people. Many patients had sites outside the classical areas. This variability is the main argument for mapping each patient individually rather than trusting anatomy.

Mechanistically, bipolar 50-60 Hz stimulation causes a local "virtual lesion" lasting only as long as the stimulus. It does not simply excite neurons, and it spreads both along the surface and across connections. A negative site therefore means "no reproducible deficit at this current," not proof that the site has no function. Thresholds are raised stepwise until a response or afterdischarges appear. Testing each site about three times reduces false positives caused by fatigue or seizure-like spread.

Subcortical mapping uses the same probe on the walls of the resection cavity. It identifies white matter tracts such as the corticospinal tract, the arcuate fasciculus and the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. With monopolar train-of-five stimulation, the motor threshold scales roughly with distance to the corticospinal tract, about 1 mA per mm in a commonly cited rule of thumb. Teams often stop resecting near thresholds of about 2-3 mA.

For MEP monitoring, the classic Kothbauer-Deletis approach uses D-waves recorded from an epidural electrode during intramedullary spinal cord tumor surgery. These are direct corticospinal volleys that are relatively resistant to anesthesia. Losing muscle MEPs while the D-wave stays above about 50% of baseline predicts temporary rather than permanent weakness. Phase reversal of the cortical SSEP N20/P20 across the central sulcus identifies the motor strip without any stimulation.

A continuing debate concerns evidence. Most data are observational, and randomized trials of IONM are rare. Its value in routine spine surgery is still disputed.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the strongest evidence supports awake mapping in diffuse low-grade glioma. A meta-analysis by De Witt Hamer and colleagues (J Clin Oncol 2012) found fewer late severe deficits with stimulation mapping despite more eloquent tumor locations. The same analysis found a higher rate of gross total resection. The field has moved from anatomical resection toward **supramaximal**, functionally bounded resection. Duffau's "onco-functional" approach removes tissue right up to the positive sites and tracts, and relies on neuroplasticity, sometimes across staged surgeries.

Pitfalls a neurophysiologist watches for:
- **False negatives** caused by currents too low, sleepy patients, poorly chosen tasks or low baseline naming accuracy. Testing should use only pictures the patient named correctly before surgery.
- **Non-surgical signal changes**: low blood pressure, hypothermia, a bolus of anesthetic, limb positioning, or brain shift moving electrodes. Real-time checklists separate these causes from true surgical injury.
- **Negative mapping with a large craniotomy**: because no positive sites were found, there are no landmarks to confirm the test worked. Many centers now use small "negative mapping" exposures only when the method has been validated at that site.
- **Seizures**: their risk rises with frontal tumors and prior seizures. They can derail awake cases, so cold Ringer's solution must be ready.

Tasks are expanding beyond naming. Mapping now targets semantic association, bilingual languages, calculation, spatial awareness via line bisection, and cognitive control. These aim to preserve higher functions that matter for quality of life and return to work. Asleep alternatives include monopolar MEP mapping of motor tracts, dorsal column mapping, and corticocortical evoked potentials, where single pulses map connectivity, such as the arcuate fasciculus, without requiring patient participation.

Open questions include:
- What is the true causal value of IONM in elective spine surgery, which needs pragmatic trials?
- Can stimulation results be standardized across centers, for example with shared atlases of positive sites?
- Can high-gamma ECoG mapping of passive responses replace stimulation in children or in patients who cannot cooperate? It is promising, but high-gamma activity marks participation in a task, not necessity for it.
- Can mapping be combined with tractography and intraoperative MRI to correct for brain shift?

keyPoints: IONM records evoked potentials and EMG during surgery to catch reversible injury
MEPs test motor (corticospinal) pathways; SSEPs test the dorsal column sensory pathway
Anesthesia choice matters: TIVA is preferred, and neuromuscular blockers abolish MEPs and EMG
Cortical stimulation creates a brief virtual lesion to find essential cortex
Awake mapping detects speech arrest or naming errors at language sites
Language sites are small and vary between people, so each patient is mapped individually

test.q: What does a motor evoked potential (MEP) primarily assess?
test.explain: MEPs stimulate the motor cortex and record muscle responses, so they test the corticospinal tract. SSEPs, not MEPs, test the dorsal columns.

test.q: Why can SSEP monitoring alone miss a new postoperative weakness?
choices: SSEPs measure blood flow, not signals
SSEPs work under deep sedation alone
SSEPs test sensory, not motor, tracts
SSEPs are recorded from muscles directly
test.explain: SSEPs travel in the dorsal columns, so an injury to the motor pathway can occur while SSEPs remain normal.

test.q: Which drug class abolishes MEPs and EMG signals during surgery?
test.explain: Neuromuscular blockers stop transmission at the neuromuscular junction, so no muscle response can be recorded.

test.q: During awake language mapping, a site is labeled positive when stimulating it:
choices: Produces a visual flash of light
test.explain: Language sites are identified by reproducible task disruption such as speech arrest or naming errors.

test.q: Which classic technique uses 50-60 Hz bipolar stimulation of the cortex?
test.explain: The Penfield technique delivers 50-60 Hz biphasic pulses through a bipolar probe. Train-of-five uses short high-frequency trains through a monopolar probe.

test.q: Afterdischarges on ECoG during stimulation mainly warn of:
test.explain: Afterdischarges are seizure-like activity that can progress to a clinical seizure.

test.q: How is a stimulation-induced seizure commonly stopped on the exposed cortex?
test.explain: Cold irrigation, such as cold Ringer's solution, rapidly suppresses focal seizures caused by stimulation.

test.q: Which anesthetic approach is generally preferred during MEP monitoring?
test.explain: Total intravenous anesthesia, for example propofol and remifentanil, depresses evoked potentials less than volatile agents. Paralytics abolish MEPs.

test.q: Which approach lets surgeons remove brain tumors near speech areas while preserving language?
test.explain: In an awake craniotomy the patient performs language tasks during stimulation mapping, so essential sites can be identified and spared.

test.q: EMG records ___ activity to warn of nerve irritation during surgery.
test.explain: Electromyography records muscle activity, which rises when the nerve supplying the muscle is irritated.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for intraoperative neuromonitoring?
test.explain: IONM stands for intraoperative neuromonitoring.

test.q: Which Montreal neurosurgeon pioneered cortical stimulation mapping in awake patients?
test.explain: Wilder Penfield's work in the 1930s-50s produced the homunculus and early speech arrest maps.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors listen to brain signals during surgery?
choices: To help the patient fall asleep
To make the surgery go faster
kidTest.explain: If a signal fades, the surgeon knows to stop and protect that part.

kidTest.q: Why is a patient sometimes awake during brain surgery?
choices: So the surgeon can ask for tools
So they can help test talking
So they can watch the surgeon
kidTest.explain: Being awake lets the patient name pictures, so doctors can find the talking spots.

kidTest.q: What does the doctor do to test a spot on the brain?
choices: Gives it a tiny, safe buzz
Shines a bright light on it
kidTest.explain: A small electrical buzz briefly turns the spot off so doctors can see what it does.

kidTest.q: If a buzz stops the patient from naming a picture, the surgeon:
kidTest.explain: That spot helps with talking, so it is kept safe.

kidTest.q: Some brain parts help you t _ _ _. (hint: speak)
kidTest.explain: Language areas help you talk, and mapping protects them.

advancedTest.q: A site shows no deficit at the current used. The most accurate interpretation is:
choices: The site certainly has no function and is safe to remove
No reproducible deficit here, which does not prove no function
The stimulator failed, so the result should be ignored
The site is a language area that tolerated the stimulus well
advancedTest.explain: Stimulation creates a temporary virtual lesion. A negative result depends on current, task and patient state, so it does not prove the site lacks function.

advancedTest.q: During spinal cord tumor surgery, muscle MEPs disappear but the D-wave stays near baseline. This most likely predicts:
choices: A sensory loss with intact motor function
Permanent paraplegia that will not recover
An anesthetic artifact with no clinical effect
advancedTest.explain: A D-wave preserved above about 50% of baseline means corticospinal axons are intact, so loss of muscle MEPs predicts temporary weakness.

advancedTest.q: Why do Ojemann's findings argue for mapping each patient individually?
choices: Stimulation reliably reveals a single language center
Broca's area lies in an identical spot in everyone
Imaging by itself pinpoints the essential language sites
Language sites are small and vary widely in location
advancedTest.explain: Essential sites were about 1-2 cm² and varied between people, often lying outside classical areas, so anatomy alone cannot be trusted.

advancedTest.q: Why is passive high-gamma ECoG mapping not yet a full replacement for stimulation?
choices: It fails to record cortical signals during speech
It reflects task participation rather than necessity
It needs much higher stimulation currents than mapping
It works mainly in patients under deep anesthesia
advancedTest.explain: High-gamma activity shows which areas take part in a task. Stimulation tests whether disrupting an area causes a deficit, which is what predicts harm from removal.
